headline: Peanut Bunker Squeeze Into the Harbors — Bass and Blues Crowd the Doorways
subhead: A steep temperature drop from Kings Point to New London is stacking bait tight in the western bays, and the stripers know exactly where to find the buffet.
body_markdown:
I spent three mornings this week doing more watching than casting, and that's fine by me — the bait tells you everything before the rods do. Right now the peanut bunker are pushed up tight into the corners of Cold Spring Harbor and Oyster Bay, balled up so thick under the terns that the surface looks like it's simmering even though the water itself isn't doing much. Diving birds over a nervous patch of bunker in eight feet of water at first light is about as honest a signal as this Sound gives you, and this week it's been reliable almost daily inside those western harbors.

Here's why. Kings Point is reading 71 degrees, New London is sitting at 67.5 — that's a real gradient stretched across roughly seventy miles of water, and it means the western half of my beat is running warmer and holding bait tighter than the central and eastern stretches. Bunker and peanuts don't love getting flushed out into open, cooler water when there's a warm, protected pocket to sit in. So they're piling into the back bays — Huntington, Lloyd Harbor, Cold Spring, upper Oyster Bay — and the bass are following them in on the tide rather than chasing bait out on the flood the way they might in a more uniform thermal year.

The pattern that's actually working: fish the second half of the outgoing tide in those shallow, mud-bottom pockets. As the water drains off the flats it drags warmer surface water and bait with it, and that's where the current edges and seams form — right where the bass want to sit and let the buffet come to them. I've had the best luck with 3-inch white or bone Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1/2-ounce bucktails, worked slow along the drop where the mud gives way to the channel. Nothing fancy, no need to punch it far — these are close-quarters fish holding tight to structure and current breaks. Slot fish have been the bulk of it, with enough 28- to 30-inch bass mixed in to keep it interesting. A few reports of overslot fish pushing 34, 35 inches came out of the Huntington back bay complex, which tells me there's real size mixed into that bait push, not just resident schoolies.

Out on the open Sound, Stratford Shoal is still doing what it always does this time of year — concentrating everything that swims through the narrows. The rip there on the tide change has been holding bluefish, and they're not small — choppers in the 5- to 8-pound range have been busting bait on top hard enough that you can spot the blitz from a half mile off. Small poppers and 1-ounce metal, cast right into the froth on the drop, have been getting hit almost every cast when the rip is really working. Middle Ground Light has had a similar bluefish presence, though more scattered — worth a pass if you're running that direction anyway.

Fluke have been a more honest, grind-it-out story. The flats west of Port Jefferson and around the edges of Stratford Shoal in 20 to 35 feet are producing keepers, but you're working for them — a lot of shorts mixed in, and you need to cover water on the drift to find the pockets holding size. White Gulp paired with a chartreuse bucktail teaser has been my go-to, dragged slow along bottom on the last of the ebb when the current isn't ripping you off the structure too fast. Nobody's filling a cooler in twenty minutes right now, but a patient drift with bait-tipped rigs will put a few keeper fluke in the boat.

Porgies are thick around the Norwalk Islands and off Charles Island — that part hasn't changed and probably won't through August. Sandworms or clam on a simple high-low bottom rig in 15 to 25 feet on the incoming tide is still the formula, and it's about as close to a sure thing as this Sound offers right now. Weakfish have shown up as a bycatch surprise in a few of those same back-bay bass spots — nothing to plan a trip around yet, just scattered fish in the mix, which is worth noting since weakfish numbers have been thin the past few seasons.

Blackfish are off the table for now with the summer closure in effect on both sides of the Sound, so I haven't been chasing them, and neither should you.

Looking ahead, I'm watching the bait more than the forecast. If that peanut bunker push holds in the western harbors through this week's tide cycle, I'd keep working the ebb in Oyster Bay and Cold Spring Harbor — that's where the highest percentage of quality bass has been coming from. The Stratford Shoal rip should keep firing blues as long as that current keeps ripping through the narrows on the tide change; that's a spot that rewards showing up right at the turn and leaving if the boils go quiet. And I'm starting to check the sand eel situation daily now — no sign of bonito yet, but this is roughly the window when the first scouts start showing on the Norwalk Islands side most years, and the bait patterns this week suggest the Sound's getting primed for it. I wouldn't plan a trip around bonito just yet, but I'd have a light spinning rod rigged and ready before I head out.
